title: Sequences and recurrences
blurb: Linear recurrences and the characteristic equation, integer terms from nonlinear recurrences, periodicity, sharp bounds, strong induction, and recurrences hidden in counting.
outcomes: Solve linear recurrences, including repeated and complex roots, and use the roots to prove properties of the terms
Prove that a nonlinear recurrence gives integers by finding a hidden linear recurrence
Use periodicity modulo m, power comparisons and counting models to answer questions about sequences
lesson:
Prove that $\lfloor(2+\sqrt3)^n\rfloor$ is odd for every $n\ge1$. Put $a_n=(2+\sqrt3)^n+(2-\sqrt3)^n$. Both $2\pm\sqrt3$ are roots of $x^2-4x+1$, so $a_{n+2}=4a_{n+1}-a_n$ with $a_0=2$ and $a_1=4$. Hence every $a_n$ is an even integer. Since $0<(2-\sqrt3)^n<1$, we get $\lfloor(2+\sqrt3)^n\rfloor=a_n-1$, which is odd.

De Moivre solved linear recurrences in 1730, and Euler and Lagrange gave the characteristic equation used below. School courses stop at arithmetic and geometric sequences. Olympiad problems expect three further habits, and this unit is built around them. Replace a nonlinear recurrence by a linear one, read a recurrence modulo $m$, and compare a sequence with a power of itself to get sharp bounds. You will use all three in the practice problems.

Linear recurrences

Theorem 1. Let $c_k\neq0$ and $p(x)=x^k-c_1x^{k-1}-\dots-c_k$. The sequences with \[a_{n+k}=c_1a_{n+k-1}+\dots+c_ka_n\quad(n\ge0)\] form a vector space of dimension $k$, and each is fixed by $a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}$. If $r$ is a root of $p$ of multiplicity $m$, the sequences $n^jr^n$ with $0\le j<m$ are solutions, and these $k$ sequences, taken over all roots, form a basis. In particular, if $p$ has distinct roots $r_1,\dots,r_k$, then $a_n=A_1r_1^n+\dots+A_kr_k^n$.

Proof. Let $E$ be the shift, $(Ea)_n=a_{n+1}$, so the recurrence reads $p(E)a=0$. The map $a\mapsto(a_0,\dots,a_{k-1})$ is a bijection, which gives the dimension. Write $p(x)=q(x)(x-r)^m$. Then \[(E-r)\bigl(n^jr^n\bigr)=r^{n+1}\bigl((n+1)^j-n^j\bigr),\] which is $r^n$ times a polynomial of degree $j-1$, so $(E-r)^m$ kills $n^jr^n$ for $j<m$.

For independence, suppose $\sum_iP_i(n)r_i^n=0$ for all $n$, with distinct roots $r_i$ (all nonzero as $c_k\neq0$) and polynomials $P_i$ not all zero, and choose such a relation with the least total degree. A single term $P(n)r^n=0$ forces $P=0$. Otherwise apply $E-r_1$. The term with $r_1$ becomes $r_1^n\cdot r_1\bigl(P_1(n+1)-P_1(n)\bigr)$, of smaller degree, while for $i\neq1$ the term $P_i(n)r_i^n$ becomes $Q_i(n)r_i^n$ with $Q_i$ of the same degree as $P_i$ and leading coefficient multiplied by $r_i-r_1\neq0$. This is a smaller nontrivial relation, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

Only the independence argument has real content. If you are happy to take the basis on trust, read on and come back to the proof later. What you must know is the statement, and in particular the factor $n^j$ for a repeated root.

For real sequences, a pair of complex roots $\rho e^{\pm i\theta}$ gives the real solutions $\rho^n\cos n\theta$ and $\rho^n\sin n\theta$.

Integer terms from nonlinear recurrences

Lemma 2 (linearisation). Let $a_0,a_1,\dots$ be nonzero with $a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2=C$ for all $n\ge1$, where $C$ is a constant. Then $K=\frac{a_{n+1}+a_{n-1}}{a_n}$ does not depend on $n$, so $a_{n+1}=Ka_n-a_{n-1}$.

Proof. Subtracting the relations for $n$ and $n+1$ gives $a_{n+2}a_n-a_{n+1}^2=a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2$, that is $a_n(a_{n+2}+a_n)=a_{n+1}(a_{n+1}+a_{n-1})$. Divide by $a_na_{n+1}$. $\blacksquare$

If $K$ and the first two terms are integers, every term is an integer. The lemma is short, but spotting the constant $C$ in a problem is the hard part, so always compute $a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2$ for the first few terms. The same subtraction works when the relation has extra terms, as in Problem 1.

Periodicity

Theorem 3. (1) If $a_{n+k}$ is determined modulo $m$ by $a_n,\dots,a_{n+k-1}$ modulo $m$, then $(a_n\bmod m)$ is eventually periodic. If also $a_n$ is determined modulo $m$ by $a_{n+1},\dots,a_{n+k}$, the sequence is periodic from the start. (2) If the characteristic polynomial $p$ divides $x^N-c$, then $a_{n+N}=c\,a_n$ for all $n$.

Proof. (1) There are $m^k$ possible windows $(a_n,\dots,a_{n+k-1})\bmod m$, so two windows agree, and from then on the sequence repeats. Running the recurrence backwards carries the repetition back to $n=0$. (2) If $x^N-c=p(x)q(x)$, then $(E^N-c)a=q(E)p(E)a=0$. $\blacksquare$

For instance $a_{n+2}=-a_{n+1}-a_n$ has $p(x)=x^2+x+1$, a factor of $x^3-1$, so every solution has period $3$. A linear recurrence with integer coefficients and $c_k=\pm1$ can always be run backwards modulo $m$, so part (1) gives a period from the start.

Recurrences in counting

To count objects of size $n$, condition on the last piece. Tilings of a $1\times n$ strip by squares and dominoes end in a square or a domino, so their number $f_n$ satisfies $f_n=f_{n-1}+f_{n-2}$, and $f_n$ is the Fibonacci number $F_{n+1}$.

When removing the last piece leaves a shape of a different kind, give that shape its own sequence and write a system. For tilings of a $2\times n$ board by dominoes and L-trominoes, the second sequence counts boards with one corner cell missing. Once the recurrence is known, Theorem 1 gives a closed form and Theorem 3 gives residues.

The other direction is just as useful. A recurrence with positive integer coefficients often counts something, and a count can be read in a second way, by symmetry or by rotation, as in Problem 6.

Bounds and strong induction

This is the least mechanical part of the unit, since the right comparison has to be guessed. For $a_{n+1}=a_n+f(a_n)$ with $f$ small, look for a power $k$ such that $a_{n+1}^k-a_n^k$ is almost constant, then add up, as in Example 3. A bounded monotone sequence converges, which we quote from analysis. When $a_n$ depends on many earlier terms, assume the claim for every smaller index (strong induction).

How to spot the method

  1. A linear recurrence with constant coefficients. Write down $p(x)$ and its roots.
  2. A quotient such as $\frac{a_n^2+5}{a_{n-1}}$ that should be an integer. Look for a constant combination, then use Lemma 2.
  3. A question about residues, or a recurrence that looks trigonometric. Look for a period.
  4. An estimate of $a_{1000}$. Compare $a_{n+1}^k$ with $a_n^k$.
  5. A counting problem with a size $n$. Condition on the last piece to get a recurrence.

Worked examples

Example 1. Let $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+2}=2a_{n+1}-4a_n$. Prove that $a_n=0$ if $3\mid n$ and $|a_n|=2^{n-1}$ otherwise.

The terms begin $0,1,2,0,-8,-16,0,64$, which suggests $a_{n+3}=-8a_n$. To prove the guess, apply the recurrence twice: \[a_{n+3}=2a_{n+2}-4a_{n+1}=2(2a_{n+1}-4a_n)-4a_{n+1}=-8a_n.\] So $a_{3j}=0$, $a_{3j+1}=(-8)^j$ and $a_{3j+2}=2(-8)^j$, which gives $|a_n|=2^{n-1}$ when $3\nmid n$.

Theorem 3(2) explains the guess. The roots of $x^2-2x+4$ are $1\pm i\sqrt3=2e^{\pm i\pi/3}$, so $x^2-2x+4$ divides $x^3+8$. Theorem 1 gives the formula $a_n=\frac{2^n}{\sqrt3}\sin\frac{n\pi}{3}$ as well.

Remark. The cube of each root is $-8$, and that is where the period $3$ and the factor $-8$ come from.

Example 2. Let $a_0=1$, $a_1=2$ and $a_{n+1}=\dfrac{a_n^2+5}{a_{n-1}}$ for $n\ge1$. Prove that every term is an integer and that consecutive terms are coprime.

A direct induction would need $a_{n-1}\mid a_n^2+5$, which says nothing about how $a_{n-1}$ and $a_n$ are related. Instead, every term is positive, since numerator and denominator are, and the definition says $a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2=5$. So Lemma 2 applies, and $a_2=9$ gives $K=\frac{9+1}{2}=5$, that is \[a_{n+1}=5a_n-a_{n-1}.\] Hence all terms are integers.

A common divisor of $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$ divides $a_{n+1}a_{n-1}-a_n^2=5$. Modulo $5$ the recurrence reads $a_{n+1}\equiv-a_{n-1}$, so the residues run $1,2,4,3,1,2,\dots$ and are never $0$. Hence consecutive terms are coprime. $\blacksquare$

Remark. The constant $5$ was never used beyond being constant. Any recurrence of this shape is linear in disguise.

Example 3. Let $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n+\dfrac{2}{a_n^2}$. Find $\lfloor a_{1000}\rfloor$.

Adding up the increments $\frac2{a_n^2}$ directly goes nowhere, since each increment depends on the term we are trying to estimate. Since $(a^3)'=3a^2$, cube instead: \[a_{n+1}^3=a_n^3+6+\frac{12}{a_n^3}+\frac{8}{a_n^6}.\] Hence $a_n^3\ge1+6(n-1)=6n-5$, and $a_{1000}^3\ge5995>18^3=5832$.

For the upper bound, $a_k^3\ge6k-5\ge k$ gives $\frac{12}{a_k^3}+\frac{8}{a_k^6}\le\frac{20}{k}$, so with $H_N=1+\frac12+\dots+\frac1N\le1+\ln N$, \[a_{1000}^3\le5995+20H_{999}\le5995+20(1+\ln999)<5995+159<19^3=6859.\] So $\lfloor a_{1000}\rfloor=18$.

Remark. The power $3$ is chosen so that the main term of $a_{n+1}^3-a_n^3$ is constant. The error terms are then summable with room to spare.

Example 4. A staircase of $n$ steps is climbed by steps of $1$ or $2$, never two $2$s in a row, and $c_n$ is the number of ways ($c_0=1$). Prove that every positive integer is a sum of distinct numbers $c_k$, $k\ge1$, whose indices pairwise differ by at least $3$.

The recurrence is the easy half. Condition on the last step. If the last step is $1$, the rest is any climb of $n-1$ steps. If the last step is $2$ and $n\ge3$, the step before is $1$, and the rest is any climb of $n-3$ steps. So $c_n=c_{n-1}+c_{n-3}$ for $n\ge3$, with $c_0=c_1=1$ and $c_2=2$, giving $1,2,3,4,6,9,13,19,\dots$ for $k\ge1$, increasing.

We prove by strong induction on $N\ge1$ that $N$ has such a representation in which every index $j$ satisfies $c_j\le N$. Let $c_k\le N<c_{k+1}$. If $N=c_k$ we are done. Otherwise $k\ge3$, since $c_2-c_1=c_3-c_2=1$, and \[0<N-c_k<c_{k+1}-c_k=c_{k-2}.\] By the induction hypothesis $N-c_k$ is a sum of terms $c_j$ with $c_j<c_{k-2}$, so $j\le k-3$. Adding $c_k$ keeps the indices at least $3$ apart. $\blacksquare$

Remark. With gap $2$ and Fibonacci numbers this is Zeckendorf's theorem. The greedy choice works because the recurrence says exactly how much room is left.

Common traps.

  • A repeated root $r$ needs $nr^n$ as well as $r^n$, or two initial values cannot be matched.
  • Lemma 2 divides by $a_n$, so prove first that no term is $0$.
  • A pattern in the first terms is a conjecture until you prove the recurrence behind the pattern.
  • Eventual periodicity is not periodicity. Check that the recurrence can be run backwards.
  • In a bound, name each inequality you use, such as $H_N\le1+\ln N$.

practice.q: Let $a_1=a_2=1$ and $a_{n+2}=\dfrac{a_{n+1}^2+a_{n+1}+1}{a_n}$ for $n\ge1$. Prove that every term is an integer, and that $3\mid a_n$ if and only if $3\mid n$.
practice.hint: The quantity $a_{n+2}a_n-a_{n+1}^2-a_{n+1}$ is constant. Subtract two consecutive instances, as in Lemma 2.
practice.sol:
This is Lemma 2 with an extra term, and the only question is whether the subtraction still works. By induction every term is a positive real number. For $n\ge1$ the definition reads \[a_{n+2}a_n-a_{n+1}^2-a_{n+1}=1.\] Equating this with the same relation for $n+1$ gives $a_{n+3}a_{n+1}+a_{n+1}^2+a_{n+1}=a_{n+2}^2+a_{n+2}a_n+a_{n+2}$, that is \[a_{n+1}(a_{n+3}+a_{n+1}+1)=a_{n+2}(a_{n+2}+a_n+1).\]

So $k_n=\frac{a_{n+2}+a_n+1}{a_{n+1}}$ satisfies $k_{n+1}=k_n$. As $a_3=3$, $k_1=\frac{3+1+1}{1}=5$, and \[a_{n+2}=5a_{n+1}-a_n-1\quad(n\ge1).\] Since $a_1$ and $a_2$ are integers, induction shows that every term is an integer. The sequence begins $1,1,3,13,61,291$.

Modulo $3$ the recurrence reads $a_{n+2}\equiv2a_{n+1}+2a_n+2$, and each pair of consecutive residues fixes the next. The residues of $a_1,\dots,a_5$ are $1,1,0,1,1$, so $(a_4,a_5)\equiv(a_1,a_2)$ and the residues repeat with period $3$. Hence $3\mid a_n$ exactly when $3\mid n$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. The term $a_{n+1}$ in the numerator survives only as the constant $-1$. The subtraction of Lemma 2 needs nothing more than a relation of the same shape at consecutive indices.

practice.q: Find all real numbers $x_0$ for which the sequence defined by $x_{n+1}=x_n^2-2$ has infinitely many negative terms.
practice.hint: If $|x_0|\le2$, write $x_0=2\cos2\pi t$ and look at the binary digits of $t$.
practice.ans: $x_0=2\cos r\pi$, where $r$ is not of the form $\frac{p}{2^k}$ with $p$ and $k$ integers
practice.sol:
The case $|x_0|>2$ is routine. If $|x_0|>2$, then $x_1=x_0^2-2>2$, and $x>2$ implies $x^2-2>2$. So every term after $x_0$ is positive.

Let $|x_0|\le2$ and write $x_0=2\cos2\pi t$ with $0\le t\le\frac12$. Since $(2\cos u)^2-2=2\cos2u$, induction gives $x_n=2\cos(2\pi\cdot2^nt)$. Let $f_n$ be the fractional part of $2^nt$. Then $x_n<0$ if and only if $\frac14<f_n<\frac34$.

If $t=\frac{p}{2^k}$ with integers $p$ and $k\ge0$, then $f_n=0$ and $x_n=2$ for all $n\ge k$, so only finitely many terms are negative.

Otherwise the binary expansion $t=0.d_1d_2d_3\ldots$ is unique and the digits are not eventually constant. Now $f_n=0.d_{n+1}d_{n+2}\ldots$ in binary, so $f_n\in[\frac14,\frac12]$ when $d_{n+1}d_{n+2}=01$ and $f_n\in[\frac12,\frac34]$ when $d_{n+1}d_{n+2}=10$. The endpoints $\frac14$ and $\frac34$ cannot occur, as $f_n$ is not of the form $\frac{p}{2^k}$ either. Two adjacent digits differ for infinitely many $n$, and each such $n$ gives $x_n<0$.

So the answer is $x_0=2\cos2\pi t$ with $t$ not of the form $\frac p{2^k}$, that is $x_0=2\cos r\pi$ with $r=2t$ not of this form. $\blacksquare$

Remark. The substitution turns $x\mapsto x^2-2$ into the shift of the binary digits of $t$. A negative term is a pair of adjacent digits that differ, and only the angles whose digits end in zeros escape.

practice.q: Find all real numbers $c$ for which there is a bounded sequence of integers $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$, not all zero, with $a_{n+2}=c\,a_{n+1}-a_n$ for all $n\ge0$.
practice.hint: First show that $c$ is rational. If $c=\frac pq$ in lowest terms, which terms must be divisible by $q$? Then bound $|c|$ with the characteristic roots.
practice.sol:
Step 1. The recurrence can be run backwards, $a_n=c\,a_{n+1}-a_{n+2}$. So if two consecutive terms are $0$, every term is $0$. In particular some $a_{n+1}\neq0$, and $c=\frac{a_{n+2}+a_n}{a_{n+1}}$ is rational.

Step 2. This is the step that needs an idea. Write $c=\frac pq$ with $q\ge1$ and $\gcd(p,q)=1$. From $q(a_{n+2}+a_n)=p\,a_{n+1}$ we get $q\mid a_{n+1}$ for every $n\ge0$. So $b_n=\frac{a_{n+1}}{q}$ is again a bounded integer sequence satisfying the recurrence, and not all zero by Step 1. Repeating, $q^j\mid a_n$ for all $n\ge j$. If $q\ge2$, choose $j$ with $q^j$ larger than every $|a_n|$. Then $a_n=0$ for all $n\ge j$, which contradicts Step 1. So $q=1$ and $c$ is an integer.

Step 3. Suppose $|c|\ge3$. The roots of $x^2-cx+1$ are real, $r$ and $\frac1r$ with $|r|>1$, so by Theorem 1, $a_n=Ar^n+Br^{-n}$. Boundedness forces $A=0$, because $|A||r|^n\le|a_n|+|B|$. Then $|a_n|=|B||r|^{-n}<1$ for large $n$, so $a_n=0$ for large $n$, against Step 1. Hence $|c|\le2$.

Step 4. Each remaining value works. For $c=2$ take $1,1,1,\dots$, for $c=-2$ take $1,-1,1,-1,\dots$, for $c=1$ take $0,1,1,0,-1,-1,\dots$ (period $6$), for $c=0$ take $0,1,0,-1,\dots$ (period $4$), and for $c=-1$ take $0,1,-1,0,1,-1,\dots$ (period $3$). So $c\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Step 2 replaces Niven's theorem, which says that if $\theta$ is a rational multiple of $\pi$ and $2\cos\theta$ is rational, then $2\cos\theta\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. Divisibility alone forces $c$ to be an integer.

practice.q: Let $a_1$ be a positive integer and $a_{n+1}=a_n+\left\lfloor\dfrac{a_n}{\lfloor\sqrt{a_n}\rfloor}\right\rfloor$ for $n\ge1$. Determine all $a_1$ for which the sequence contains a perfect square, and prove that the sequence then contains infinitely many.
practice.hint: Write $a_n=m^2+r$ with $m=\lfloor\sqrt{a_n}\rfloor$ and $0\le r\le2m$. Find what two steps do to $r$ when $r<m$.
practice.sol:
Every positive integer $a$ is uniquely $m^2+r$ with $m=\lfloor\sqrt a\rfloor\ge1$ and $0\le r\le2m$, and then $\lfloor a/m\rfloor=m+\lfloor r/m\rfloor$.

Two steps when $r<m$. The figure shows the two steps. Then $\lfloor a/m\rfloor=m$, and the next term is $m^2+m+r$. This is less than $(m+1)^2$, so the floor of the square root is still $m$, and dividing by $m$ gives $m+1+\frac rm$, with floor $m+1$. So the term after is $(m+1)^2+r$. Hence the terms alternate between $M^2+e$ and $M^2+M+e$ for consecutive $M$, with $e=r$ fixed and $e<M$ throughout.

The other cases. If $m\le r<2m$, then $a=m^2+m+e$ with $e=r-m<m$, which is the second kind of term, and the step gives $(m+1)^2+e$ as before. If $r=2m$, then $\lfloor a/m\rfloor=m+2$ and the next term is $(m+1)^2+(m+1)$, the second kind of term with $e=0$. So from $a_1$ or $a_2$ on the sequence follows the pattern, where $e=r$ if $r<m$, $e=r-m$ if $m\le r<2m$, and $e=0$ if $r=2m$, for $a_1=m^2+r$.

Squares. The numbers $M^2+e$ and $M^2+M+e$ with $0\le e<M$ lie in $[M^2,(M+1)^2)$, so such a term is a square only when the term is $M^2$, that is $e=0$ and the term is of the first kind. If $e=0$, every other term is a square. If $e\ge1$, then $a_1$ is already in the pattern and no term is a square.

So the sequence contains a square if and only if $e=0$, that is $r\in\{0,m,2m\}$ and $a_1\in\{m^2,\,m^2+m,\,m^2+2m\}$, and then the sequence contains infinitely many squares. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Finding the invariant offset $e$ is the whole problem. A good first experiment is $a_1=5$, which gives $5,7,10,13,17,21,26,\dots$ with $e=1$.

practice.q: Let $\alpha$ be the largest real root of $x^3-7x^2+1=0$. Prove that $\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not a perfect square for any positive integer $n$.
practice.hint: Show that $\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor=s_n-1$, where $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$th powers of the three roots. Then use one modulus for even $n$ and another for odd $n$.
practice.sol:
Two facts are standard, that the other two roots are small and that the power sums are integers. The real problem is choosing the moduli. Let $f(x)=x^3-7x^2+1$. Then $f(-\frac12)=-\frac78$, $f(0)=1$, $f(\frac12)=-\frac58$, $f(6)=-35$ and $f(7)=1$, so the roots satisfy \[-\tfrac12<\gamma<0<\beta<\tfrac12,\qquad 6<\alpha<7.\] Also $\beta+\gamma=7-\alpha>0$, so $\beta>|\gamma|$. For $n\ge1$ this gives $\beta^n+\gamma^n\ge\beta^n-|\gamma|^n>0$ and $\beta^n+\gamma^n<2\cdot2^{-n}\le1$.

Let $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$. Each root satisfies $x^{n+3}=7x^{n+2}-x^n$, so $s_{n+3}=7s_{n+2}-s_n$, with $s_0=3$, $s_1=7$ and $s_2=7^2-2\cdot0=49$ by Vieta. So every $s_n$ is an integer, $s_n-1<\alpha^n<s_n$, and $\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor=s_n-1$.

Even $n$. Modulo $5$ the recurrence is $s_{n+3}\equiv2s_{n+2}-s_n$. The residues of $s_0,s_1,\dots,s_6$ are $3,2,4,0,3,2,4$, so the residues have period $4$, and $s_n-1$ is $2$ or $3$ modulo $5$ for $n\equiv0$ or $2\pmod4$. A square is $0$, $1$ or $4$ modulo $5$.

Odd $n$. Modulo $7$ the recurrence is $s_{n+3}\equiv-s_n$, so the residues of $s_0,s_1,s_2,\dots$ run $3,0,0,4,0,0,3,\dots$ with period $6$. For odd $n$ this gives $s_n-1\equiv6$ when $3\nmid n$ and $s_n-1\equiv3$ when $n\equiv3\pmod6$. A square is $0$, $1$, $2$ or $4$ modulo $7$.

So $\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor=s_n-1$ is never a square. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Neither modulus works alone. Modulo $5$ the odd $n$ give the residues $1$ and $4$, and modulo $7$ the index $n=6$ gives $2$, all squares.

practice.q: Let $s_1=1$, $s_2=1$, $s_3=4$ and $s_n=s_{n-1}+s_{n-3}$ for $n\ge4$. Prove that $s_p-1$ is divisible by $p$ for every prime $p$.
practice.hint: For $n\ge4$, $s_n$ counts the tilings of a ring of $n$ cells by single cells and blocks of three consecutive cells. Rotate the ring by one cell.
practice.sol:
The recurrence alone gives no reason for $p$ to divide $s_p-1$. The idea is to find something that $s_n$ counts and then rotate. A model for $s_n$. Place $n\ge4$ cells around a circle and tile them by single cells and by blocks of three consecutive cells. Let $c_n$ be the number of tilings, and let $t_m$ be the number of tilings of a row of $m$ cells by the same pieces, so $t_0=t_1=t_2=1$ and $t_m=t_{m-1}+t_{m-3}$ for $m\ge3$ (condition on the last piece). In a ring tiling, cell $1$ is either a single cell, leaving a row of $n-1$ cells, or lies in one of the three blocks $\{n-1,n,1\}$, $\{n,1,2\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$, which are different as $n\ge4$, each leaving a row of $n-3$ cells. So \[c_n=t_{n-1}+3t_{n-3}.\]

For $n\ge7$ the recurrence for $t$ gives \[c_n-c_{n-1}-c_{n-3}=(t_{n-1}-t_{n-2}-t_{n-4})+3(t_{n-3}-t_{n-4}-t_{n-6})=0.\] Also $s_4=5$, $s_5=6$, $s_6=10$, while $c_4=t_3+3t_1=5$, $c_5=t_4+3t_2=6$ and $c_6=t_5+3t_3=10$. Hence $c_n=s_n$ for all $n\ge4$.

Small primes. $s_2-1=0$ and $s_3-1=3$.

Rotation. Let $p\ge5$ be prime and let $\rho$ rotate the ring by one cell. Then $\rho$ permutes the $c_p$ tilings and $\rho^p$ is the identity, so each orbit $\{T,\rho T,\rho^2T,\dots\}$ has size dividing $p$, that is $1$ or $p$. If $\rho T=T$, then $T$ is fixed by every rotation. Should $T$ contain a block $\{j,j+1,j+2\}$, the block $\{j+1,j+2,j+3\}$ would also be in $T$, and the two blocks are different but overlap, which is impossible. So the only fixed tiling is the one by single cells, and \[s_p=c_p=1+p\cdot(\text{number of orbits of size }p)\equiv1\pmod p.\] So $p$ divides $s_p-1$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. In algebraic terms $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$ for the roots of $x^3-x^2-1$, and $s_p\equiv(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^p=1$. The rotation proof needs no algebra, only a model in which the recurrence counts something.
